A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization. Image-only content was visually inspected.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.5 report original data-dropping and refitting analyses on Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench, including numerical ranking changes and inspections of influential evaluations.

after.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original ranking analyses on LLM and sports datasets, bootstrap and random-deletion experiments, and a GPT-5.1-assisted qualitative study.

M1.justification: v1 excludes ties and analyzes unweighted Bradley–Terry models; v2 adapts the framework to weighted models with win/loss weight 2 and tie weight 1 (Section 2, Appendix C.2). This changes the fitted objective and supported outcomes, while retaining the AMIP subset search, pairwise-to-top-k procedure, optional additive one-step Newton approximation and exact refitting.

E1.justification: v2 retains Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench and adds search-augmented dialogue, web development and visual question answering through Search, Webdev and Vision Arenas. NBA team rankings and ATP tennis player rankings add distinct non-LLM domains (Section 4.1, Appendix D).

E2.justification: Appendix A.3 and Table 3 introduce an evaluated uniform-at-random deletion control for comparison with targeted worst-case deletion. This comparator is absent from v1; the newly cited leaderboard attacks are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Retaining tied preferences changes the existing evaluation samples, including Chatbot Arena human judgments from 39,716 to 57,477. v2 also introduces bootstrap-based top-set evaluation, random deletion at 1% and an additional 0.1% Chatbot condition, sports filtering protocols, competitor-removal experiments and GPT-5.1 judging procedures (Appendices A, D and F).

E4.justification: v2 adds bootstrap-ranking robustness checks, random-deletion controls, competitor-removal tests of score-margin sensitivity and explicit verification of AMIP-selected subsets. It replaces v1's five manually inspected examples with two cases assessed by GPT-5.1. The player-involvement analysis is updated in Appendix E, while the original score-gap scatterplot is retained as Figure 18.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates and deletion counts without uncertainty intervals or repeated-trial results. v2 Appendix A adds bootstrap confidence-interval plots and stability estimates from 100 random-deletion trials. Bootstrap resample counts, confidence levels and seeds remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes Chatbot Arena human results from 9/39,716 deletions to 2/57,477 and MT-Bench human results from 83/2,575 to 92/3,355. These use revised tie handling, so they are not same-setting robustness gains. v2 adds results for five datasets and several new analyses, while removing v1's head-to-head win percentages. Some reports conflict internally: v2 Table 2 gives 40/2,400 as 4.00%, and Section 4.4 and Appendix F disagree on the GPT-4 model involved in the inspected losses.

T1.justification: v2 formalizes the weighted tie-handling objective and logistic representation, and introduces the bootstrap-based rank and top-set criterion. Pairwise reversal changes from the non-strict inequality in v1 Equation (8) to a strict inequality in v2 Equation (7). The top-k proposition and proof are retained as Proposition B.1, as are the logistic influence formula and complexity bound.

C1.justification: The central claims of a fast robustness diagnostic and ranking sensitivity to very few preferences remain. v2 broadens the stated scope to Bradley–Terry variants and Arena derivatives, and qualifies the human-versus-LLM conclusion from being 'just as sensitive' to neither being systematically more sensitive (abstract and Section 4.3).

C2.justification: v2 explicitly explains that unsuccessful searches cannot certify robustness and that masking can cause false negatives (Appendix H). Appendix A distinguishes worst-case sensitivity from sampling uncertainty. v1's five examples motivate a similar-response explanation, whereas v2's two new examples motivate an outlier-preference interpretation, although Section 4 retains the old similarity statement. Score-margin mechanisms and benchmark-design implications are also expanded.

D1.justification: v2 adds weighted-model implementation details, dataset identifiers and sports filtering instructions, exact deleted indices in Table 4, and the GPT-5.1 judging prompt and access mode. It removes v1's public-code and reproduction-scripts statement and repository link; this does not establish that the repository itself was withdrawn. The hardware and runtime disclosure is retained.

R1.justification: Section 5 substantially expands positioning relative to vote manipulation, attacks on LLM judges and apathetic annotations, adding works including Huang et al. (2025b), Raina et al. (2024) and Zhao et al. (2025). Additional uncertainty-quantification and masking literature broadens the statistical context. The earlier comparison with Shiffman et al. is retained.

P1.justification: The introduction and discussion are substantially rewritten. v1's platform-deviations subsection is incorporated into the setup, while proofs, logistic formulations, dataset descriptions and case analyses are redistributed across appendices. A dedicated related-work section and extensively reorganized appendix narrative change the document's structure beyond the scientific additions.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a denser conference layout and adds a conceptual schematic, pseudocode, paired bootstrap-interval plots, sports ranking plots and random-deletion and verification tables. Table 1 is restructured, and v1's five-example table is replaced by full-response figures and judge-output blocks. Existing involvement and model-count plots are relocated or redrawn; the score-gap plot is largely retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1 by incorporating tied preferences, evaluating confidence-interval-based rankings and distinguishing targeted fragility from random-deletion stability. Explicit false-negative and masking limitations also clarify what the diagnostic establishes. These substantially strengthen applicability and evidential support, despite the removed code link and unresolved numerical and model-attribution inconsistencies in Table 2 and Section 4.4/Appendix F.
